scenario: A 17-year-old boy has inflammatory acne on the face and trunk. He has used adapalene nightly for 8 weeks with partial improvement and still has many inflamed papules. He is not pregnant, has no tetracycline allergy, and plays outdoor sports. The clinician is choosing how to add an oral antibiotic.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?
options: Doxycycline alone, stopped only when the skin is clear for 12 months
Doxycycline plus benzoyl peroxide, with a plan to stop the antibiotic near 3 months
Oral isotretinoin started the same week as doxycycline
Topical clindamycin monotherapy continued indefinitely
Monthly azithromycin pulses without a topical agent
correctAnswer: Doxycycline plus benzoyl peroxide, with a plan to stop the antibiotic near 3 months
explanation: Doxycycline plus benzoyl peroxide, with a plan to stop the antibiotic near 3 months is correct. The 2024 AAD acne guideline strongly recommends benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, and oral doxycycline, and it limits systemic antibiotics. Benzoyl peroxide is paired with the antibiotic to reduce resistance, and the antibiotic course is measured in months rather than continued until some future clear year. Incorrect alternatives: Indefinite doxycycline, clindamycin alone, and azithromycin pulses without a topical partner all extend antibiotic exposure. Isotretinoin plus a tetracycline raises the risk of pseudotumor cerebri and is not how isotretinoin is started.

references.label: Reynolds RV et al. Guidelines of care for the management of acne vulgaris. J Am Acad Dermatol 2024

scenario: A 20-year-old woman has nodulocystic acne with scarring after 4 months of doxycycline, tretinoin, and benzoyl peroxide. She is not pregnant, uses two contraceptive methods, and has a normal mood screen. A colleague suggests monthly complete blood counts and basic metabolic panels for the whole course because 'isotretinoin always needs them.'
question: Which of the following best matches current acne-guideline practice for this patient?
options: Start isotretinoin and order baseline liver enzymes and lipids, repeating them if abnormal or if a dose change warrants it
Continue doxycycline for another year before considering isotretinoin
Start isotretinoin and a daily tetracycline together for the first 8 weeks
Defer isotretinoin because scarring alone is not an indication if some papules remain
Order a pregnancy test once at the first visit and not again
correctAnswer: Start isotretinoin and order baseline liver enzymes and lipids, repeating them if abnormal or if a dose change warrants it
explanation: Start isotretinoin and order baseline liver enzymes and lipids, repeating them if abnormal or if a dose change warrants it is correct. The 2024 AAD guideline strongly recommends oral isotretinoin for acne that is severe, scarring, psychosocially burdensome, or failing standard therapy. Baseline liver enzymes and fasting lipids are obtained; routine population-wide monthly blood counts and chemistry panels are not required in otherwise healthy patients. Incorrect alternatives: Waiting another year of antibiotic after scarring has already occurred misses the indication. A tetracycline is not combined with isotretinoin. Pregnancy testing is repeated in patients who can become pregnant; one test is not the program.

blueprintTopic: Perioral dermatitis after a topical steroid
scenario: A 28-year-old woman has 6 weeks of burning papules around the mouth and in the nasolabial folds, sparing a thin clear zone at the vermilion border. She has been applying a mid-potency topical steroid nightly, which helps for a day and then the rash returns worse. There are no comedones.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate first change in treatment?
options: Continue the steroid and add oral prednisone for 3 weeks
Stop the topical steroid and start topical metronidazole or a calcineurin inhibitor
Start oral isotretinoin the same day the steroid is stopped
Apply clobetasol to the folds for 2 weeks to break the cycle
Treat with permethrin because the distribution proves scabies
correctAnswer: Stop the topical steroid and start topical metronidazole or a calcineurin inhibitor
explanation: Stop the topical steroid and start topical metronidazole or a calcineurin inhibitor is correct. Perioral dermatitis is often sustained by topical corticosteroids. Stopping the steroid and using a nonsteroid anti-inflammatory topical, sometimes with a tetracycline, is the usual first plan. Incorrect alternatives: More steroid, including clobetasol in the folds or a prednisone taper, feeds the rebound. Isotretinoin is not first-line for this limited eruption. The spared vermilion border and steroid history are not the burrows of scabies.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 46-year-old man has central facial erythema, telangiectasias, and papules without comedones. He also has gritty eyes, lid margin crusting, and recurrent styes. A student proposes oral isotretinoin first because the cheeks look 'phymatous,' but there is no bulbous nasal change.

Topical metronidazole or ivermectin, lid hygiene, and ophthalmology if the eye symptoms persist
A 6-week course of oral prednisone
Topical clobetasol to the eyelids
Excision of the telangiectasias before any medical therapy
correctAnswer: Topical metronidazole or ivermectin, lid hygiene, and ophthalmology if the eye symptoms persist
explanation: Topical metronidazole or ivermectin, lid hygiene, and ophthalmology if the eye symptoms persist is correct. Papulopustular rosacea is treated with topical anti-inflammatory agents, and ocular disease is managed with lid care and eye referral rather than jumping to isotretinoin. Isotretinoin is reserved for more refractory or phymatous disease. Incorrect alternatives: A steroid on the lids can worsen ocular surface disease and periorificial eruptions. Prednisone and surgery are not the opening treatment for this phenotype.

scenario: A 33-year-old man started amoxicillin yesterday. Today he has fever of 39 C and hundreds of pinpoint nonfollicular pustules on edematous erythema in the axillae and groin. options: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
Generalized pustular psoriasis
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
correctAnswer: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
explanation: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis is correct. AGEP starts within 1 to 2 days of a beta-lactam, favors flexures, and is a sterile neutrophilic pustular eruption without eosinophilia or necrolysis. Incorrect alternatives: DRESS needs a latency of weeks, eosinophilia, facial edema, and organ injury. SJS has mucosal erosions. Pustular psoriasis is not timed to one dose of a new antibiotic. Staphylococcal scalded skin is a tender superficial peel, usually in a child, not flexural pustules.

scenario: A 44-year-old man with known plaque psoriasis has bright red, sharply bordered, glistening plaques in the gluteal cleft and axillae. Potassium hydroxide preparation is negative. He has been using clobetasol in the folds for 6 weeks and the skin is thinning.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate change?
options: Continue clobetasol daily for another 8 weeks
Switch to topical tacrolimus or a short course of a low-potency steroid, and stop the superpotent steroid
Start oral terbinafine for presumed tinea
Start methotrexate today because any fold plaque requires a systemic drug
Apply nystatin powder indefinitely
correctAnswer: Switch to topical tacrolimus or a short course of a low-potency steroid, and stop the superpotent steroid
explanation: Switch to topical tacrolimus or a short course of a low-potency steroid, and stop the superpotent steroid is correct. Inverse psoriasis lacks scale in moist folds. Superpotent steroids cause atrophy and striae there, so a calcineurin inhibitor or a brief low-potency steroid is preferred. Incorrect alternatives: A negative potassium hydroxide preparation and the psoriasis history make tinea and candida unlikely, so terbinafine or endless nystatin is the wrong turn. A limited fold plaque does not by itself require methotrexate.

scenario: A 7-year-old Black boy has a 6-week patch of scale and broken hairs with occipital lymphadenopathy. A sibling has a similar patch. A caregiver has been using minoxidil foam because an online post called it alopecia areata.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue minoxidil for 6 months before any test
Potent topical steroid monotherapy
Potassium hydroxide or fungal culture, then oral terbinafine or griseofulvin
Intralesional triamcinolone today
Topical ketoconazole shampoo as the only treatment
correctAnswer: Potassium hydroxide or fungal culture, then oral terbinafine or griseofulvin
explanation: Potassium hydroxide or fungal culture, then oral terbinafine or griseofulvin is correct. Scale, broken hairs, lymphadenopathy, and a household contact point to tinea capitis, which needs an oral antifungal because topical agents do not reach the hair shaft. Incorrect alternatives: Minoxidil and intralesional steroid treat alopecia areata and will miss a spreading dermatophyte. Shampoo alone does not cure the shaft infection.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 61-year-old man wants oral terbinafine for three thickened yellow great toenails. He has no skin scale. He takes simvastatin and drinks little alcohol. Liver enzymes last year were normal.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate step before the prescription?
options: Start a 12-week course today based on the nail appearance
Confirm fungus with potassium hydroxide, stain, or culture, and check baseline liver enzymes
Combine oral terbinafine with daily itraconazole
Use oral ketoconazole because it needs no monitoring
Treat with topical ciclopirox for 1 week only
correctAnswer: Confirm fungus with potassium hydroxide, stain, or culture, and check baseline liver enzymes
explanation: Confirm fungus with potassium hydroxide, stain, or culture, and check baseline liver enzymes is correct. Many dystrophic nails are not dermatophyte. Confirmation avoids a hepatotoxic course, and a baseline liver panel is appropriate before terbinafine, especially with a statin. Incorrect alternatives: Appearance alone misclassifies psoriasis, trauma, and mold. Stacking azoles, using oral ketoconazole, or a 1-week lacquer course are not acceptable substitutes.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 54-year-old man with diabetes has 10 hours of severe pain in the perineum out of proportion to a small dusky patch. He is toxic, heart rate is 124/min, and crepitus is palpable. Glucose is 340 mg/dL and lactate is 4.1 mmol/L.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next management?
options: Oral cephalexin and clinic follow-up tomorrow
Immediate surgical exploration with broad intravenous antibiotics
A 48-hour trial of intravenous vancomycin alone before any surgeon is called
Incision and drainage in the clinic if fluctuance appears
Topical mupirocin and elevation
correctAnswer: Immediate surgical exploration with broad intravenous antibiotics
explanation: Immediate surgical exploration with broad intravenous antibiotics is correct. Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, crepitus, and a dusky perineal patch are Fournier gangrene until proved otherwise. Source control is surgical and cannot wait on a day of antibiotics. Incorrect alternatives: Oral cephalexin, topical mupirocin, and clinic drainage treat uncomplicated cellulitis or an abscess. Vancomycin alone misses gram-negative and anaerobic organisms in perineal necrotizing infection.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 19-year-old man has 3 days of target lesions on the extremities and a few oral erosions after a recurrent herpes labialis outbreak. Body surface detachment is under 10%, Nikolsky sign is negative, and he is hemodynamically stable. He started no new drug.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate classification and first step?
options: Toxic epidermal necrolysis; transfer to a burn unit and give intravenous immunoglobulin as the only therapy
Erythema multiforme, treat the herpes recurrence, and stop any unnecessary drug, without calling this SJS
DRESS; start systemic steroids for 6 weeks
Pemphigus vulgaris; start rituximab today
Staphylococcal scalded skin; start nafcillin only
correctAnswer: Erythema multiforme, treat the herpes recurrence, and stop any unnecessary drug, without calling this SJS
explanation: Erythema multiforme, treat the herpes recurrence, and stop any unnecessary drug, without calling this SJS is correct. Typical targets on acral skin after herpes, with limited mucosal erosions and no sheet-like detachment, are erythema multiforme. Herpes-associated disease is treated by addressing the virus and supportive care. Incorrect alternatives: SJS/TEN is a drug necrolysis syndrome with atypical targets and more extensive detachment. DRESS has eosinophilia and organ injury after weeks of a drug. Pemphigus and scalded skin do not follow this herpes-timed target pattern.

scenario: A 76-year-old man has 2 months of tense bullae on the thighs and a flexor urticarial prodrome. Nikolsky sign is negative. Oral mucosa is spared. He takes no new medicines.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pemphigus vulgaris
Bullous pemphigoid
Dermatitis herpetiformis
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Porphyria cutanea tarda
correctAnswer: Bullous pemphigoid
explanation: Bullous pemphigoid is correct. Tense bullae, a negative Nikolsky sign, elderly age, and spared mucosa fit subepidermal bullous pemphigoid. Incorrect alternatives: Pemphigus has flaccid bullae, a positive Nikolsky sign, and often starts in the mouth. Dermatitis herpetiformis is intensely pruritic and grouped on elbows and knees. SJS is an acute drug necrolysis. Porphyria favors dorsal hands and is associated with hepatitis or alcohol, not tense thigh bullae in this pattern.

scenario: A 27-year-old man has 10 days of oval, scaly, salmon plaques on the trunk, including the palms. He had a painless penile ulcer 6 weeks ago that healed. He is sexually active with new partners.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next test?
options: Reassurance that a herald patch makes biopsy unnecessary
Serum RPR or treponemal testing before calling this pityriasis rosea
Potassium hydroxide preparation only
Patch testing for nickel
Antinuclear antibody as the first test
correctAnswer: Serum RPR or treponemal testing before calling this pityriasis rosea
explanation: Serum RPR or treponemal testing before calling this pityriasis rosea is correct. Palm and sole involvement plus a recent chancre makes secondary syphilis the diagnosis to exclude. Pityriasis rosea spares palms and soles. Incorrect alternatives: A herald-patch story does not override palm lesions and a chancre. Fungal prep, nickel testing, and ANA do not evaluate this systemic infection.

scenario: A 49-year-old woman has a 7-mm dark brown macule on the calf that has become irregular and multicolored over 4 months. A clinician wants tissue before a wide excision.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate biopsy?
options: Superficial shave that samples only the epidermis
Narrow excisional biopsy through the subcutis, oriented along the relaxed skin lines
Punch of the lightest edge only
Curettage and electrodesiccation as diagnosis and treatment
Cryotherapy without histology
correctAnswer: Narrow excisional biopsy through the subcutis, oriented along the relaxed skin lines
explanation: Narrow excisional biopsy through the subcutis, oriented along the relaxed skin lines is correct. A suspected melanoma needs a full-thickness sample so Breslow depth can be measured. A narrow excision does that and still allows later wide margins. Incorrect alternatives: A superficial shave or a punch of the pale edge can miss the deepest tumor. Curettage and cryotherapy destroy the architecture and are not diagnostic.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 72-year-old fair-skinned farmer has several rough, sandpaper-like erythematous macules on the bald scalp. They are easier to feel than to see. A nearby stuck-on brown plaque with horn cysts is asymptomatic.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate statement about the rough scalp lesions?
options: They are seborrheic keratoses and need no treatment
They are actinic keratoses, a premalignant lesion treated with cryotherapy or a field agent
They are melanoma and require sentinel-node biopsy now
They are tinea and need oral terbinafine
They are bullous pemphigoid and need prednisone
correctAnswer: They are actinic keratoses, a premalignant lesion treated with cryotherapy or a field agent
explanation: They are actinic keratoses, a premalignant lesion treated with cryotherapy or a field agent is correct. Gritty sun-exposed lesions are actinic keratoses and can progress to squamous cell carcinoma. The stuck-on plaque is the seborrheic keratosis, a different lesion. Incorrect alternatives: Seborrheic keratoses are waxy and stuck-on, not sandpaper macules. Melanoma, tinea, and pemphigoid do not match this texture.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 29-year-old woman has recurrent boils in both axillae with sinus tracts and a scarred bridged plaque, but no systemic sepsis today. Incision of individual nodules has been done four times this year and they return. She is not pregnant.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying direction?
options: Repeated incision of every nodule as the only long-term plan
Stop tobacco, start an anti-inflammatory antibiotic or biologic strategy, and refer for deroofing of the sinus tracts
A 10-day course of cephalexin each month indefinitely
Topical benzoyl peroxide as the sole therapy for tract disease
Oral isotretinoin combined with a tetracycline
correctAnswer: Stop tobacco, start an anti-inflammatory antibiotic or biologic strategy, and refer for deroofing of the sinus tracts
explanation: Stop tobacco, start an anti-inflammatory antibiotic or biologic strategy, and refer for deroofing of the sinus tracts is correct. Hurley II disease with sinus tracts is not cured by serial incision. Anti-inflammatory antibiotics, and for more extensive disease a TNF inhibitor, plus surgical deroofing, address the tunnels. Incorrect alternatives: Cephalexin pulses and benzoyl peroxide alone do not close sinus tracts. Isotretinoin plus a tetracycline is the wrong combination and is not first-line for tunnels.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 35-year-old man and his partner have nocturnal pruritus and burrows in the finger webs. He used permethrin once from the neck down and washed it off at 6 hours. His partner was not treated. One week later he is still itching and has new burrows.
question: Which of the following best explains the failure?
options: Permethrin never works and ivermectin is mandatory for ordinary scabies
The cream was removed too soon and the untreated partner reinfested him
The itch at one week proves treatment failure even if burrows are gone
Steroids should replace the scabicide
The rash is pityriasis rosea and permethrin was irrelevant
correctAnswer: The cream was removed too soon and the untreated partner reinfested him
explanation: The cream was removed too soon and the untreated partner reinfested him is correct. Permethrin is left on about 8 to 14 hours and repeated in a week, and close contacts are treated together. New burrows mean living mites, not just post-scabetic itch. Incorrect alternatives: Ordinary scabies does not require ivermectin first; crusted scabies does. Itch can persist after cure, but new burrows do not. Steroids and a pityriasis label ignore the burrows.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 22-year-old woman has 48 hours of pruritic follicular pustules on the trunk and buttocks that began the day after sitting in a poorly chlorinated hot tub. She is afebrile and otherwise well.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?
options: Incision of every pustule and intravenous vancomycin
Reassurance that Pseudomonas folliculitis is usually self-limited, and avoid the tub until it is properly treated
Oral ketoconazole for 6 weeks
Immediate isotretinoin
Permethrin for the household
correctAnswer: Reassurance that Pseudomonas folliculitis is usually self-limited, and avoid the tub until it is properly treated
explanation: Reassurance that Pseudomonas folliculitis is usually self-limited, and avoid the tub until it is properly treated is correct. Hot-tub folliculitis from Pseudomonas is uncomfortable but typically resolves without antibiotics in a healthy host. The exposure is the clue. Incorrect alternatives: Vancomycin, long azoles, isotretinoin, and permethrin treat other diseases and do not fix the water source.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 68-year-old man has a painful vesicular rash on the tip of the nose and the forehead, respecting the midline. The eye is red and he reports photophobia. Symptoms began yesterday.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Topical steroid drops from the primary clinician without an eye exam
Oral valacyclovir started now and same-day ophthalmology evaluation
Observation because Hutchinson sign is only a skin finding
Oral acyclovir started after the rash has crusted
A shingles vaccine dose today as treatment
correctAnswer: Oral valacyclovir started now and same-day ophthalmology evaluation
explanation: Oral valacyclovir started now and same-day ophthalmology evaluation is correct. Vesicles on the nasal tip mean nasociliary involvement and a real risk of keratitis. Antiviral therapy is most useful when started early, and the cornea needs a slit lamp. Incorrect alternatives: Steroid drops without an exam can worsen herpes keratitis. Waiting for crusts misses the treatment window. Vaccine is prevention, not treatment of active zoster.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 31-year-old man has 30 umbilicated facial and groin papules that have spread for 3 months. He has had thrush once. He has never had an HIV test.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step beyond local treatment?
options: Reassurance that widespread adult molluscum needs no systemic evaluation
HIV antigen/antibody testing
Oral terbinafine
A skin biopsy before any counseling
Isotretinoin
correctAnswer: HIV antigen/antibody testing
explanation: HIV antigen/antibody testing is correct. Numerous facial molluscum in an adult is a marker of impaired cellular immunity until HIV is excluded. Incorrect alternatives: Local destruction can still be offered, but skipping the HIV test is the error. Terbinafine and isotretinoin do not treat poxvirus. Biopsy is optional when the umbilicated look is classic.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 74-year-old woman with venous insufficiency has bilateral reddish-brown, itchy, scaly skin above the medial malleoli for 2 months. Both legs are involved equally. She is afebrile, and there is no unilateral expanding warmth.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Intravenous vancomycin for bilateral cellulitis
Compression and a topical corticosteroid for stasis dermatitis
Oral terbinafine for 12 weeks
Systemic prednisone for bullous pemphigoid
Incision of the pigmented skin
correctAnswer: Compression and a topical corticosteroid for stasis dermatitis
explanation: Compression and a topical corticosteroid for stasis dermatitis is correct. Chronic bilateral medial-malleolar ochre dermatitis is venous stasis, not infection. Compression addresses the edema and a mild steroid settles the itch. Incorrect alternatives: Cellulitis is almost never bilateral and symmetric. Antifungals, pemphigoid therapy, and incision do not treat venous hypertension.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 40-year-old man spilled hot oil on the dorsum of his dominant hand 2 hours ago. The area is white, dry, and insensate, about 2% of body surface, with surrounding moist blisters that blanch slowly. He has no inhalation injury.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate disposition for the white insensate area?
options: Outpatient silicone dressing only, because any hand burn under 5% can stay home
Burn-center referral because a full-thickness burn of the hand needs specialty care
Immediate split-thickness skin graft in the clinic
Topical silver and a 2-week wait before any referral decision
Oral cephalexin as the main treatment
correctAnswer: Burn-center referral because a full-thickness burn of the hand needs specialty care
explanation: Burn-center referral because a full-thickness burn of the hand needs specialty care is correct. A white, dry, insensate burn is full thickness. Hand burns, even when small, are a standard reason for burn-center referral. Incorrect alternatives: Size under 5% does not override location and depth. Clinic grafting and a 2-week delay are not the primary-care plan. Antibiotics do not treat the depth.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 82-year-old man who has been bedbound has a sacral wound with full-thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat is visible, but bone, tendon, and muscle are not. Slough is minimal and there is no purple intact skin.
question: Which of the following is the correct stage?
options: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
Deep-tissue pressure injury
correctAnswer: Stage 3
explanation: Stage 3 is correct. Stage 3 is full-thickness skin loss that may show fat but not bone, tendon, or muscle. Incorrect alternatives: Stage 1 is intact nonblanchable erythema. Stage 2 stops at the dermis. Stage 4 exposes bone, tendon, or muscle. Deep-tissue injury is persistent purple or maroon intact skin or a blood blister.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 16-year-old boy with a BMI of 36 kg/m2 has velvety hyperpigmented plaques on the neck and axillae. He has no diarrhea or cancer symptoms. Fasting glucose is 112 mg/dL.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next evaluation?

Assessment for insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes
Skin biopsy before any laboratory test
Oral ketoconazole
Reassurance that the finding is only cosmetic and needs no metabolic test
correctAnswer: Assessment for insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes
explanation: Assessment for insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes is correct. Acanthosis nigricans in an adolescent with obesity is a skin sign of insulin resistance. An impaired fasting glucose already supports that evaluation. Incorrect alternatives: Malignant acanthosis is rare and usually sudden in an older adult with weight loss. Biopsy and antifungals are not the first step, and calling it purely cosmetic skips the glucose problem.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 19-year-old woman started doxycycline for acne 5 days ago and spent a day at the beach. She now has burning erythema on the nose, forearms, and dorsal hands in a sharp swimsuit pattern, with nail-area tenderness. She has no mucosal erosions.
question: Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
options: Stevens-Johnson syndrome from the first doses
Doxycycline phototoxicity
Allergic contact dermatitis to the ocean
Porphyria cutanea tarda
Lupus malar rash
correctAnswer: Doxycycline phototoxicity
explanation: Doxycycline phototoxicity is correct. Tetracyclines cause exaggerated sunburn in exposed skin, often within days of starting the drug. Incorrect alternatives: SJS has mucosal necrolysis and targetoid detachment, not a swimsuit sunburn. Contact allergy is not limited to the sun-exposed edge of a new tetracycline. Porphyria and acute cutaneous lupus have different chronic contexts.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 25-year-old woman has 20 minutes of generalized hives, lip swelling, wheeze, and a blood pressure of 86/50 mm Hg after a bee sting. She is still talking.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate drug?
options: Diphenhydramine intramuscularly as the only drug
Epinephrine intramuscularly in the mid-anterolateral thigh
Oral prednisone before any other drug
Ranitidine intravenously as first-line therapy
A topical steroid to the hives
correctAnswer: Epinephrine intramuscularly in the mid-anterolateral thigh
explanation: Epinephrine intramuscularly in the mid-anterolateral thigh is correct. Hypotension with wheeze and hives is anaphylaxis. Intramuscular epinephrine is the first drug and should not be delayed for antihistamines or steroids. Incorrect alternatives: Antihistamines and steroids do not reverse airway edema or shock. A topical steroid does nothing for this emergency.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 47-year-old man has intensely pruritic, polygonal, purple, flat-topped papules on the wrists with white lacy lines on the buccal mucosa. He has no new drugs.
question: Which of the following associated test is most appropriate?
options: Hepatitis C antibody
Rapid plasma reagin as the only test, because Wickham striae are syphilitic
Skin scraping for scabies as the first and only test
Colonoscopy for a juvenile polyp syndrome
Serum tryptase
correctAnswer: Hepatitis C antibody
explanation: Hepatitis C antibody is correct. The purple polygonal papules and Wickham striae are lichen planus, which is associated with hepatitis C and should prompt that test. Incorrect alternatives: Secondary syphilis can mimic many rashes but does not own this classic lichen-planus morphology. Scabies has burrows. Tryptase evaluates mast-cell disease. Colonoscopy is unrelated.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 2-day-old term infant, feeding well and afebrile, has blotchy erythematous macules with tiny central pustules on the trunk. Palms and soles are spared. The rash was absent at birth. Wright stain of a pustule shows many eosinophils.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Intravenous acyclovir
Reassurance that erythema toxicum neonatorum resolves without treatment
Oral fluconazole
Isolation for congenital candidiasis
A full sepsis evaluation because every neonatal pustule is infection
correctAnswer: Reassurance that erythema toxicum neonatorum resolves without treatment
explanation: Reassurance that erythema toxicum neonatorum resolves without treatment is correct. Erythema toxicum appears after birth in a well term infant, spares palms and soles, and the pustules are eosinophilic. Incorrect alternatives: Herpes and candida are not eosinophilic and the infant is well. Congenital infections more often present at birth and involve palms or soles. A sepsis workup is not required for this classic picture.

scenario: A 5-year-old girl has three honey-colored crusted patches on the chin. She is afebrile, and there is no cellulitis. She has no drug allergies.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Topical mupirocin
Intravenous vancomycin
Oral terbinafine
Permethrin
A superpotent steroid
correctAnswer: Topical mupirocin
explanation: Topical mupirocin is correct. Limited nonbullous impetigo in a well child is treated with topical mupirocin. Oral antibiotics are for numerous lesions or when topical therapy is impractical. Incorrect alternatives: Intravenous vancomycin is for severe resistant infection. Terbinafine, permethrin, and steroids treat fungus, scabies, and dermatitis, not streptococcal or staphylococcal crusts.

scenario: A 44-year-old woman has a urine dipstick that reads 'trace blood' at a wellness visit. She has no pain, no visible blood, and no urinary symptoms. Microscopy was not done. A colleague wants to book cystoscopy because the dipstick was positive.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Cystoscopy and CT urography this week
Microscopic urinalysis; do not diagnose microhematuria from the dipstick alone
Start nitrofurantoin for 5 days
Reassure her that trace blood never needs microscopy
Schedule a renal biopsy
correctAnswer: Microscopic urinalysis; do not diagnose microhematuria from the dipstick alone
explanation: Microscopic urinalysis; do not diagnose microhematuria from the dipstick alone is correct. The 2025 AUA/SUFU guideline defines microhematuria as more than 3 red cells per high-power field on microscopy of a properly collected specimen. A positive dipstick only triggers that microscopy. Incorrect alternatives: Cystoscopy and CT are not the response to an unconfirmed dipstick. Antibiotics and renal biopsy have no target here. Skipping microscopy leaves the dipstick uninterpreted.

scenario: A 36-year-old woman, never a smoker, has 6 red cells per high-power field on one microscopic urinalysis. Blood pressure and creatinine are normal. Repeat urinalysis within 6 months, not immediate cystoscopy or imaging
Cystoscopy and renal ultrasound now
Urine cytology every 3 months for 2 years
Start an alpha blocker and recheck in a year
correctAnswer: Repeat urinalysis within 6 months, not immediate cystoscopy or imaging
explanation: Repeat urinalysis within 6 months, not immediate cystoscopy or imaging is correct. She meets every 2025 low/negligible criterion: woman under 60, 3 to 10 red cells, never smoker, and no extra risk factor. That group gets a repeat urinalysis within 6 months rather than an immediate scope or scan. Incorrect alternatives: Immediate cystoscopy with CT is the high-risk path. Cystoscopy plus ultrasound is the intermediate path. Cytology surveillance and an alpha blocker do not evaluate this finding.

Cystoscopy and renal ultrasound; age alone does not place a woman in the high-risk group

No further testing after a single sample
Renal biopsy
correctAnswer: Cystoscopy and renal ultrasound; age alone does not place a woman in the high-risk group
explanation: Cystoscopy and renal ultrasound; age alone does not place a woman in the high-risk group is correct. In the 2025 amendment, women are not high risk from age alone. Age 60 or older with 3 to 10 red cells and no high-risk feature is intermediate risk, which is cystoscopy plus renal ultrasound. Incorrect alternatives: CT urography is for high-risk features such as more than 25 red cells, prior gross hematuria, or heavy smoking. Eight red cells at age 64 is not the low-risk pattern, so a 6-month delay without a scope is too little. One sample and a biopsy are not the pathway.

scenario: A 71-year-old man has 12 red cells per high-power field. He smoked 40 pack-years and quit 2 years ago. He has no flank pain. Creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. He takes aspirin 81 mg.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate evaluation?
options: Stop aspirin and repeat the urinalysis before any workup
Cystoscopy and axial upper-tract imaging
Repeat urinalysis in 6 months only
Renal ultrasound without cystoscopy
Empiric ciprofloxacin for 7 days
correctAnswer: Cystoscopy and axial upper-tract imaging
explanation: Cystoscopy and axial upper-tract imaging is correct. Age 60 or older in a man, and a greater than 30 pack-year smoking history, are high-risk features. High-risk microhematuria is evaluated with cystoscopy and axial upper-tract imaging. Aspirin does not cancel that evaluation. Incorrect alternatives: Holding aspirin and waiting, ultrasound without a scope, a 6-month delay, and antibiotics all under-evaluate a high-risk bladder and upper tract.

scenario: A 29-year-old woman had culture-proven cystitis with visible blood. She completed nitrofurantoin and is now asymptomatic. A colleague wants cystoscopy tomorrow because the first specimen had too many red cells to count.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Cystoscopy and CT urography before a follow-up urinalysis
Repeat urinalysis with microscopy after the infection has been treated
A 6-week course of ciprofloxacin
Renal biopsy
Start tamsulosin
correctAnswer: Repeat urinalysis with microscopy after the infection has been treated
explanation: Repeat urinalysis with microscopy after the infection has been treated is correct. Hematuria blamed on a urinary infection is rechecked after treatment. Persistent microhematuria is then risk-stratified. The bloody specimen during infection is not itself the staging sample. Incorrect alternatives: Immediate cystoscopy, a long quinolone course, biopsy, and an alpha blocker skip that confirmation.

scenario: A 78-year-old woman in a clinic has a urine culture with 100,000 CFU/mL of E. coli sent because the urine looked cloudy. She has no dysuria, frequency, fever, or flank pain. She is not pregnant and has no planned urologic procedure.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

No antibiotics
Ciprofloxacin for 7 days
Intravenous ceftriaxone once
A 14-day course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
correctAnswer: No antibiotics
explanation: No antibiotics is correct. The 2019 IDSA guideline recommends against treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in nonpregnant older adults. Cloudiness is not a symptom. Incorrect alternatives: Every listed antibiotic course treats a diagnosis she does not have and adds resistance and adverse effects.

scenario: A 26-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has a screening urine culture with 100,000 CFU/mL of pan-sensitive E. coli. She has no urinary symptoms. She has a penicillin allergy limited to a childhood rash she cannot describe.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
options: No antibiotics until she develops dysuria
Treat the bacteriuria with an agent safe in pregnancy and prove the culture clears
Ciprofloxacin for 3 days
Delay treatment until the third trimester
Weekly nitrofurantoin through delivery without a test of cure
correctAnswer: Treat the bacteriuria with an agent safe in pregnancy and prove the culture clears
explanation: Treat the bacteriuria with an agent safe in pregnancy and prove the culture clears is correct. Pregnancy is an exception to the 'do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria' rule because untreated bacteriuria raises the risk of pyelonephritis and adverse pregnancy outcomes. A test of cure follows treatment. Incorrect alternatives: Waiting for symptoms, using a fluoroquinolone, delaying until the third trimester, and an unmonitored drug through delivery are not the guideline approach.

scenario: A 52-year-old woman has fever of 39.2 C, a heart rate of 118/min, and left flank pain. CT shows a 6-mm left proximal ureteral stone with hydronephrosis. Creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis has white cells and nitrites. Antibiotics have just been started.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin and outpatient follow-up
Urgent decompression of the collecting system plus antibiotics
Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy in the clinic today
Potassium citrate and a 24-hour urine collection before any procedure
Observation until the fever breaks, then schedule ureteroscopy next week
correctAnswer: Urgent decompression of the collecting system plus antibiotics
explanation: Urgent decompression of the collecting system plus antibiotics is correct. An obstructing stone with sepsis is a drainage emergency. Antibiotics do not reach a closed space reliably, and expulsive therapy is for the stable patient. Incorrect alternatives: Tamsulosin, delayed ureteroscopy, clinic lithotripsy, and a metabolic workup do not decompress the infected kidney.

references.label: American Urological Association. Surgical Management of Stones: AUA Guideline. J Urol 2016

scenario: A 40-year-old man passed a calcium oxalate stone. A 24-hour urine shows high urinary calcium and normal oxalate. He has already been told to reach a high urine volume. He asks if he should stop all dairy.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate diet advice?
options: A low-calcium diet to starve the stone of calcium
Keep normal dietary calcium, limit sodium, and do not restrict calcium-containing foods
A high-oxalate diet to bind calcium
Stop fluids overnight so urine stays concentrated
Start allopurinol before any diet change
correctAnswer: Keep normal dietary calcium, limit sodium, and do not restrict calcium-containing foods
explanation: Keep normal dietary calcium, limit sodium, and do not restrict calcium-containing foods is correct. Low dietary calcium can raise oxalate absorption and does not prevent calcium stones. Normal calcium intake with sodium restriction is the dietary pattern, along with enough fluid to dilute the urine. Incorrect alternatives: A high-oxalate diet and overnight fluid restriction worsen risk. Allopurinol is for selected hyperuricosuria, not the first answer to a dairy question.

references.label: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline (2026). J Urol 2026

scenario: A 37-year-old woman has had three calcium oxalate stones. Her 24-hour urine shows low citrate and normal calcium, oxalate, and uric acid. She has no urinary infection with a urease-splitting organism. Serum potassium and creatinine are normal.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate medication?
options: Allopurinol
Potassium citrate
Hydrochlorothiazide as the only drug, despite normal urine calcium
Sodium bicarbonate tablets taken only on stone days
Acetazolamide
correctAnswer: Potassium citrate
explanation: Potassium citrate is correct. Recurrent calcium stones with low urinary citrate are treated with alkali, and potassium citrate is the usual agent. It raises citrate and urinary pH without a sodium load. Incorrect alternatives: Allopurinol targets hyperuricosuria. A thiazide is for high urine calcium. Sodium alkali adds a sodium load. Acetazolamide lowers citrate and can cause stones.

scenario: A 15-year-old boy woke with 3 hours of severe left testicular pain and vomiting. The left testis is high and horizontal, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. The emergency department can obtain a scrotal ultrasound in about 90 minutes. A urologist is in the hospital.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Wait for Doppler ultrasound before calling urology
Immediate urologic exploration rather than delaying for imaging
Oral levofloxacin and recheck tomorrow
Elevation of the testis and discharge if the pain eases
Antibiotics for epididymitis because pain that eases with elevation excludes torsion
correctAnswer: Immediate urologic exploration rather than delaying for imaging
explanation: Immediate urologic exploration rather than delaying for imaging is correct. A classic torsion presentation is a surgical diagnosis. Imaging is for uncertain cases and must not delay the operating room when the story and examination already fit. Incorrect alternatives: Antibiotics, next-day review, and the Prehn sign do not salvage a torsed testis. Relief with elevation is not specific enough to send him home.

scenario: A 22-year-old man has 2 days of gradual left scrotal pain and dysuria. He is sexually active. The testis is not high-riding, the cremasteric reflex is present, and Doppler ultrasound shows increased flow. He has no drug allergies.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline
Ciprofloxacin alone
Supportive care only
Immediate surgical exploration tonight
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 3 days
correctAnswer: Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline
explanation: Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is correct. Epididymitis in a sexually active man under 35 is treated for gonorrhea and chlamydia. Preserved flow and a present cremasteric reflex make torsion unlikely. Incorrect alternatives: A fluoroquinolone alone misses gonorrhea. Three days of trimethoprim is not the STI regimen. Surgery is for torsion, and supportive care leaves the infection untreated.

references.label: Workowski KA et al. Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021. MMWR Recomm Rep 2021

scenario: A 67-year-old man who has sex with women only has 3 days of gradual scrotal pain, fever, and dysuria. Ultrasound shows epididymitis and normal testicular flow. He has no cephalosporin or sulfa allergy. Prostate examination is very tender.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric coverage?
options: Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline for 7 days only
A fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole aimed at enteric organisms, after STI risk is considered
Penicillin for syphilis
Observation
Surgical detorsion
correctAnswer: A fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole aimed at enteric organisms, after STI risk is considered
explanation: A fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole aimed at enteric organisms, after STI risk is considered is correct. Epididymitis in older men is usually enteric, often with prostatitis, so coverage targets gram-negative bowel flora. STI therapy alone is the regimen for younger sexually active patients. Incorrect alternatives: Penicillin, observation, and detorsion do not treat this infection. The young-adult STI pair is the wrong age match when enteric organisms predominate.

scenario: A 70-year-old man with an indwelling catheter has a swollen, painful glans and a tight ring of foreskin behind the corona. The glans is dusky. He had the foreskin retracted for cleaning and it was not replaced.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Elective circumcision in 3 months with no reduction today
Manual reduction of the foreskin after compression, with urgent dorsal slit if reduction fails
Topical clotrimazole
Oral doxycycline
Observation because a retracted foreskin is the same as phimosis
correctAnswer: Manual reduction of the foreskin after compression, with urgent dorsal slit if reduction fails
explanation: Manual reduction of the foreskin after compression, with urgent dorsal slit if reduction fails is correct. Paraphimosis is a trapped foreskin that can strangulate the glans. Reduce it now. Phimosis is a foreskin that will not retract and is not this emergency. Incorrect alternatives: Waiting months, antifungal cream, and antibiotics do not restore blood flow.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 28-year-old man has a painful erection for 6 hours after injecting alprostadil. The corpora are rigid and tender. Aspiration of the corpus returns dark blood.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?
options: Ice packs and discharge with a 24-hour recheck
Corporal aspiration and irrigation, then intracavernosal phenylephrine if needed
Intracavernosal alprostadil
Oral sildenafil
Observation because drug-induced erections always resolve by 8 hours
correctAnswer: Corporal aspiration and irrigation, then intracavernosal phenylephrine if needed
explanation: Corporal aspiration and irrigation, then intracavernosal phenylephrine if needed is correct. A painful, prolonged erection with dark corporal blood is ischemic priapism. Aspiration and a sympathomimetic are the emergency treatment. More vasodilator or a PDE-5 inhibitor worsens it. Incorrect alternatives: Ice and waiting past several hours risk permanent erectile tissue injury.

scenario: A 46-year-old man has a new right-sided scrotal 'bag of worms' that does not get smaller when he lies down. The left side is normal. He has no fever.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassurance that a right varicocele never needs imaging
Imaging of the retroperitoneum for a venous-obstructing mass
Ceftriaxone and doxycycline
Immediate scrotal exploration for torsion
A trial of scrotal support for 6 months before any test
correctAnswer: Imaging of the retroperitoneum for a venous-obstructing mass
explanation: Imaging of the retroperitoneum for a venous-obstructing mass is correct. An isolated right varicocele, or one that does not collapse when supine, can be caused by venous obstruction from a retroperitoneal mass. That pattern is imaged. Incorrect alternatives: Antibiotics, torsion surgery, and a long delay do not look for obstruction. A classic left varicocele that decompresses is the benign pattern, and this is not that pattern.

scenario: A 9-month-old boy has a right testis that has never been felt in the scrotum. It is palpable in the inguinal canal. He was born at term. The left testis is descended. A parent asks about waiting until school age.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
options: Hormone injections as first-line therapy and surgery only after puberty
Orchiopexy well before 18 months of age
Observation until age 8 because descent is still likely
Removal of the normal left testis
Antibiotics for 10 days
correctAnswer: Orchiopexy well before 18 months of age
explanation: Orchiopexy well before 18 months of age is correct. A testis still undescended at this age is unlikely to arrive on its own. Orchiopexy is done in infancy, generally by 18 months, to protect fertility and allow later examination for cancer risk. Incorrect alternatives: Waiting until school age, hormones as the standard first step, removing the normal testis, and antibiotics are not the plan.

scenario: A 69-year-old man has a first episode of acute urinary retention. A catheter drains 900 mL. He has a large prostate on examination and no fever. He can be sent home with the catheter.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to start before a voiding trial?
options: Oxybutynin
An alpha blocker
Nitrofurantoin for 14 days
Finasteride as the only drug, with the voiding trial tomorrow morning
A PDE-5 inhibitor as emergency decompression
correctAnswer: An alpha blocker
explanation: An alpha blocker is correct. An alpha blocker started at the time of catheter drainage improves the chance of a successful voiding trial. It works within days. Incorrect alternatives: An anticholinergic can worsen retention. Finasteride shrinks the prostate over months and is not the drug that gets him through this week. Antibiotics and a PDE-5 inhibitor do not empty the bladder.

scenario: A 74-year-old man with frequency and urgency has a post-void residual of 280 mL and a weak stream. A clinician wants to start solifenacin alone.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate concern about that plan?
options: Solifenacin is first-line and the residual can be ignored
An antimuscarinic alone may precipitate retention when the residual is already high; treat the outlet and reassess
He needs antibiotics for 6 weeks instead
Mirabegron is contraindicated in every man with urgency
The residual proves interstitial cystitis
correctAnswer: An antimuscarinic alone may precipitate retention when the residual is already high; treat the outlet and reassess
explanation: An antimuscarinic alone may precipitate retention when the residual is already high; treat the outlet and reassess is correct. Urgency with a large residual and a weak stream is often bladder-outlet obstruction. Blocking detrusor contraction before addressing the outlet can cause retention. Incorrect alternatives: Ignoring 280 mL, a long antibiotic course, a blanket ban on beta-3 agonists, and an interstitial-cystitis label do not match this examination.

scenario: A 62-year-old man with no urinary symptoms asks for 'the prostate blood test' at a physical. He has not heard the tradeoffs. He is otherwise well and expects to live many more years.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?
options: Draw a PSA today without discussion because he is over 50
Discuss benefits and harms and order PSA only if he wants screening
Tell him screening is mandatory at 62
Tell him no man should ever discuss PSA
Biopsy the prostate first
correctAnswer: Discuss benefits and harms and order PSA only if he wants screening
explanation: Discuss benefits and harms and order PSA only if he wants screening is correct. For men 55 to 69, USPSTF recommends an individual decision after a discussion of a small mortality benefit versus false positives, biopsy, and treatment harms. Do not screen someone who does not want it. Incorrect alternatives: Mandatory testing, a refusal to discuss it, and a biopsy before any conversation are not the recommendation.

scenario: A 76-year-old man with severe heart failure and a limited life expectancy asks for a routine PSA. He has no symptoms and had a normal PSA 2 years ago. He wants whatever is 'recommended for everyone his age.'

Do not perform routine PSA screening
Go directly to prostate biopsy
Start finasteride to lower the PSA
Order a PSA every 3 months
correctAnswer: Do not perform routine PSA screening
explanation: Do not perform routine PSA screening is correct. USPSTF recommends against PSA screening at age 70 and older because harms outweigh benefits, especially when life expectancy is limited. Incorrect alternatives: Annual or quarterly testing, empiric finasteride, and an upfront biopsy are not screening recommendations for him.

scenario: A 66-year-old man on apixaban for atrial fibrillation passed visible blood in the urine once yesterday. The urine is now yellow. CT was ordered by a colleague 'only if he is not anticoagulated.'
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate statement?
options: Visible blood on an anticoagulant needs no urologic evaluation
Gross hematuria is evaluated, including cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging, whether or not he takes an anticoagulant
A single dipstick in 6 months is enough
Stop apixaban forever and skip cystoscopy
Treat with nitrofurantoin
correctAnswer: Gross hematuria is evaluated, including cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging, whether or not he takes an anticoagulant
explanation: Gross hematuria is evaluated, including cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging, whether or not he takes an anticoagulant is correct. Anticoagulation may unmask a tumor; it does not explain the blood away. Gross hematuria is a high-risk feature and is not followed like low-risk microhematuria. Incorrect alternatives: A delayed dipstick, permanently stopping anticoagulation without a workup, and an antibiotic do not find a bladder tumor.

scenario: A 58-year-old woman leaks a small amount of urine when she coughs or lifts. She does not have urgency, nocturia, or dysuria. Pelvic examination shows no fistula. Post-void residual is 20 mL.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

Pelvic floor muscle training
An indwelling catheter
Daily nitrofurantoin
Tamsulosin
correctAnswer: Pelvic floor muscle training
explanation: Pelvic floor muscle training is correct. Leakage with cough and lift, without urgency, is stress incontinence. Pelvic floor training is the initial treatment. Incorrect alternatives: An antimuscarinic treats urge incontinence. A catheter, prophylaxis, and an alpha blocker do not retrain the sphincter mechanism.

scenario: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 28 mL/min/1.73 m2 and a urine albumin-creatinine ratio of 480 mg/g. He takes losartan. Hemoglobin A1c is 7.4%. Potassium is 4.4 mEq/L. A colleague says an SGLT2 inhibitor cannot be started below an eGFR of 45.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate medication change?
options: Do not start an SGLT2 inhibitor until the eGFR is above 45
Start an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven kidney benefit
Stop losartan before any SGLT2 inhibitor
Start a sulfonylurea instead because the eGFR is under 30
Start dual ACE-inhibitor and ARB therapy
correctAnswer: Start an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven kidney benefit
explanation: Start an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven kidney benefit is correct. KDIGO 2024 and the ADA 2026 standards recommend an SGLT2 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes and CKD when the eGFR is at least 20, not 45. Kidney benefit is independent of the glucose effect. Incorrect alternatives: Waiting for an eGFR of 45 withholds a drug that slows progression. Stopping the ARB, adding a second renin-angiotensin drug, or substituting a sulfonylurea misses the kidney indication.

scenario: A 70-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria started dapagliflozin 2 weeks ago. Her eGFR fell from 48 to 42 mL/min/1.73 m2. She is eating normally, potassium is 4.6 mEq/L, and she has no volume depletion. A covering clinician wants it stopped because 'the kidneys worsened.'
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
options: Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor permanently
Continue it; an early eGFR dip is expected and is not a reason to stop
Add an NSAID for the creatinine change
Switch to glyburide
Start dialysis planning because the eGFR fell by 6
correctAnswer: Continue it; an early eGFR dip is expected and is not a reason to stop
explanation: Continue it; an early eGFR dip is expected and is not a reason to stop is correct. KDIGO notes that the early hemodynamic drop in eGFR after an SGLT2 inhibitor is generally not a reason to discontinue the drug, and monitoring frequency does not have to change just because it was started. Incorrect alternatives: Permanent cessation, an NSAID, a sulfonylurea swap, and dialysis planning treat a hemodynamic dip as kidney failure.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

blueprintTopic: Continue SGLT2 inhibitor below an eGFR of 20
scenario: A 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has been stable on empagliflozin. His eGFR has drifted from 24 to 18 mL/min/1.73 m2. He is not on dialysis, he tolerates the drug, and he has no ketosis. He is about to undergo an elective colonoscopy with a full bowel prep next month.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for the SGLT2 inhibitor?
options: Stop it forever because the eGFR is now under 20
Continue it day to day, and hold it for the prolonged fast around the procedure
Double the dose because the eGFR is lower
Replace it with metformin at an eGFR of 18
Add a second SGLT2 inhibitor
correctAnswer: Continue it day to day, and hold it for the prolonged fast around the procedure
explanation: Continue it day to day, and hold it for the prolonged fast around the procedure is correct. Once started, an SGLT2 inhibitor may be continued if the eGFR falls below 20, until kidney replacement or intolerance. It is held for prolonged fasting, surgery, or critical illness because of ketosis risk. Incorrect alternatives: Stopping forever at an eGFR of 18, doubling the dose, adding metformin below 30, or stacking two agents are not the recommendations.

Replace the ACE inhibitor with ibuprofen
correctAnswer: Continue lisinopril; a rise under 30% is acceptable
explanation: Continue lisinopril; a rise under 30% is acceptable is correct. KDIGO says to continue ACE-inhibitor or ARB therapy unless creatinine rises by more than 30% within 4 weeks. A 17% rise with a safe potassium is the expected hemodynamic effect. Incorrect alternatives: Stopping at 17%, combining ACE inhibitor with ARB, adding a mineralocorticoid antagonist without a potassium check, and substituting an NSAID are harmful turns.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

blueprintTopic: Stop the ACE inhibitor when the rise exceeds 30%
scenario: A 66-year-old woman started ramipril 2 weeks ago for proteinuric CKD. Creatinine rose from 1.5 to 2.2 mg/dL (about 47%). Potassium is 5.6 mEq/L. She has been taking ibuprofen for knee pain.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue ramipril and add ibuprofen standing doses
Hold the ACE inhibitor, stop the NSAID, and reassess volume and renal artery perfusion
Add a second ACE inhibitor
Start metformin
Ignore the change until the next annual lab
correctAnswer: Hold the ACE inhibitor, stop the NSAID, and reassess volume and renal artery perfusion
explanation: Hold the ACE inhibitor, stop the NSAID, and reassess volume and renal artery perfusion is correct. A creatinine rise above 30% is a reason to hold the renin-angiotensin drug and look for volume depletion, NSAID use, or bilateral renal-artery stenosis. The potassium of 5.6 reinforces that hold. Incorrect alternatives: Continuing through a 47% rise, stacking ACE inhibitors, starting metformin in this setting, and waiting a year leave a reversible injury in place.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

scenario: A 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily. The eGFR is now 38 mL/min/1.73 m2. She has no acidosis, hypoxia, or decompensated heart failure. Hemoglobin A1c is 7.1%.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate metformin plan?
options: Continue 2000 mg daily because lactic acidosis is rare
Reduce the total daily dose to 1000 mg and monitor kidney function
Stop metformin and start glyburide
Increase metformin because the eGFR fell
Stop all glucose-lowering drugs
correctAnswer: Reduce the total daily dose to 1000 mg and monitor kidney function
explanation: Reduce the total daily dose to 1000 mg and monitor kidney function is correct. At an eGFR of 30 to 44, metformin is not started, and if it is already in use the dose is reduced, commonly to 1000 mg daily, with closer monitoring. It is stopped below 30. Incorrect alternatives: Full dose at an eGFR of 38, a sulfonylurea substitution as the only option, a dose increase, and stopping all therapy overshoot the recommendation.

references.label: American Diabetes Association. 11. Chronic Kidney Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026. Diabetes Care 2026

scenario: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m2, and urine albumin-creatinine ratio 600 mg/g is on lisinopril and dapagliflozin. Potassium has been 4.3 and 4.5 mEq/L. A colleague suggests finerenone.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate use of finerenone here?
options: Add it, and recheck potassium, because he is already on an ACE inhibitor and an SGLT2 inhibitor with a normal potassium
Do not use it unless the potassium is above 5.5
Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor before any finerenone can be considered
Use it as a substitute for the ACE inhibitor
Start it at an eGFR of 12
correctAnswer: Add it, and recheck potassium, because he is already on an ACE inhibitor and an SGLT2 inhibitor with a normal potassium
explanation: Add it, and recheck potassium, because he is already on an ACE inhibitor and an SGLT2 inhibitor with a normal potassium is correct. KDIGO allows a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist to be added to a renin-angiotensin inhibitor and an SGLT2 inhibitor in type 2 diabetes with CKD when potassium is consistently normal, with potassium checked after the start. Incorrect alternatives: Waiting until potassium is already high, stopping the SGLT2 inhibitor, replacing the ACE inhibitor, or starting at an eGFR of 12 are not the selection rules.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

scenario: A 72-year-old man with CKD stage G4 has a venous bicarbonate of 16 mEq/L on two checks. He is euvolemic, potassium is 4.2 mEq/L, and he is not having diarrhea.
