Oral alkali to raise bicarbonate, with monitoring so it is not driven too high
Acetazolamide
A high-protein diet
Daily normal-saline boluses at home
correctAnswer: Oral alkali to raise bicarbonate, with monitoring so it is not driven too high
explanation: Oral alkali to raise bicarbonate, with monitoring so it is not driven too high is correct. KDIGO suggests treating metabolic acidosis in adults with CKD when bicarbonate is under about 18 mmol/L, and monitoring so treatment does not overshoot. Incorrect alternatives: Waiting for a bicarbonate of 10 leaves chronic bone and muscle effects. Acetazolamide, extra protein, and saline boluses worsen acid-base or volume balance.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

scenario: A 68-year-old man has 2 days of vomiting. Creatinine rose from 0.9 to 2.1 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 92/60 mm Hg. Urine sodium is 8 mEq/L, fractional excretion of sodium is 0.4%, and the sediment has hyaline casts only.
question: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?
options: Acute tubular necrosis
Prerenal azotemia from volume loss
Postrenal obstruction
Acute interstitial nephritis
Cholesterol emboli
correctAnswer: Prerenal azotemia from volume loss
explanation: Prerenal azotemia from volume loss is correct. A bland sediment, urine sodium under 20, and fractional excretion of sodium under 1% in a volume-depleted patient is prerenal physiology. The tubules are still conserving sodium. Incorrect alternatives: ATN has muddy-brown casts and a fractional excretion of sodium usually above 2%. Obstruction needs imaging clues. Interstitial nephritis has white cells, white-cell casts, and often a drug latency. Cholesterol emboli follow a procedure and show livedo or eosinophilia.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 75-year-old man was hypotensive during a gastrointestinal bleed yesterday. Today creatinine is 3.4 mg/dL, urine sodium is 46 mEq/L, and the sediment shows muddy-brown granular casts. He is now normotensive after transfusion.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Prerenal azotemia that still needs more saline
Acute tubular necrosis
Bladder outlet obstruction
Minimal-change disease
Isolated prerenal state from heart failure
correctAnswer: Acute tubular necrosis
explanation: Acute tubular necrosis is correct. Muddy-brown casts and a high urine sodium after a documented ischemic insult are the sediment of tubular injury, not ongoing prerenal conservation. Incorrect alternatives: More saline after he is resuscitated does not reverse established tubular injury. Obstruction, minimal-change disease, and heart-failure physiology have different examinations and sediments.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 62-year-old woman started pantoprazole 10 days ago and now has a creatinine of 2.8 mg/dL from a baseline of 0.8. She has a maculopapular rash and eosinophilia. Urine shows white cells and white-cell casts. Antibiotics were not given.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate first action?
options: Increase the pantoprazole dose
Stop pantoprazole
Start empiric cyclophosphamide
Begin dialysis immediately because of the rash
Add an NSAID for the rash
correctAnswer: Stop pantoprazole
explanation: Stop pantoprazole is correct. A proton-pump inhibitor is a classic cause of acute interstitial nephritis. The rash, eosinophilia, white cells, and white-cell casts after a new drug point to that diagnosis, and the drug is stopped. Incorrect alternatives: Raising the dose, adding an NSAID, or jumping to cyclophosphamide or dialysis before withdrawal treats the wrong step.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 80-year-old man has lower abdominal pain and no urine for 14 hours. Creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL. A bladder scan shows 700 mL. Kidneys were normal 2 months ago.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: High-dose furosemide
Urethral catheter drainage
Oral sodium bicarbonate only
Renal biopsy
Start an SGLT2 inhibitor
correctAnswer: Urethral catheter drainage
explanation: Urethral catheter drainage is correct. Anuria with a full bladder is postrenal obstruction until drained. Relief of the outlet comes before diuretics or disease-modifying CKD drugs. Incorrect alternatives: Furosemide, alkali, biopsy, and an SGLT2 inhibitor do not empty an obstructed bladder.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

blueprintTopic: CKD is three months, not one lab
scenario: A 55-year-old man has a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL today. Six weeks ago it was 0.9 during an illness, and he has no older results. Urine albumin-creatinine ratio is 12 mg/g. He feels well now.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate label today?
options: CKD stage G3a A1, start an SGLT2 inhibitor today
Possible acute or subacute kidney change; repeat the creatinine before diagnosing CKD
End-stage kidney disease
Nephrotic syndrome
No follow-up is needed
correctAnswer: Possible acute or subacute kidney change; repeat the creatinine before diagnosing CKD
explanation: Possible acute or subacute kidney change; repeat the creatinine before diagnosing CKD is correct. CKD requires kidney abnormalities for at least 3 months. One elevated creatinine after a recent normal value is not yet CKD, and albuminuria is absent. Incorrect alternatives: Staging him G3 and starting long-term therapy, calling it end-stage or nephrotic disease, or dropping follow-up all misread a single lab.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

scenario: Two patients both have an eGFR of 52 mL/min/1.73 m2. One has a urine albumin-creatinine ratio of 18 mg/g. The other has a ratio of 420 mg/g. Both have diabetes.
question: Which of the following is the most important difference?
options: They have the same KDIGO risk because the eGFR matches
The patient with the ratio of 420 is in a higher albuminuria category and a higher risk cell
Only the patient with the ratio of 18 needs an ACE inhibitor
Albuminuria is ignored once the eGFR is above 45
The ratio of 420 is normal
correctAnswer: The patient with the ratio of 420 is in a higher albuminuria category and a higher risk cell
explanation: The patient with the ratio of 420 is in a higher albuminuria category and a higher risk cell is correct. KDIGO classifies CKD by cause, GFR category, and albuminuria category. An eGFR of 52 is G3a, but 420 mg/g is A3 and 18 mg/g is A1, so the risk is not the same. Incorrect alternatives: Matching eGFR does not match risk. The higher albuminuria, not the lower one, is the ACE-inhibitor indication. A ratio of 420 is not normal.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

blueprintTopic: NSAID and ACE inhibitor and diuretic
scenario: A 77-year-old woman on lisinopril and chlorthalidone starts ibuprofen three times daily for osteoarthritis. Three days later creatinine has doubled and potassium is 5.8 mEq/L. She is still making urine.
question: Which of the following best explains the injury?
options: A single-drug allergy to chlorthalidone
Loss of prostaglandin dilation of the afferent arteriole on top of efferent dilation blockade and volume loss
Cholesterol emboli from the ibuprofen tablet
Minimal-change disease from the diuretic
An expected 10% creatinine change that should be ignored
correctAnswer: Loss of prostaglandin dilation of the afferent arteriole on top of efferent dilation blockade and volume loss
explanation: Loss of prostaglandin dilation of the afferent arteriole on top of efferent dilation blockade and volume loss is correct. The 'triple whammy' is an NSAID plus a renin-angiotensin blocker plus a diuretic. The NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole while the ACE inhibitor dilates the efferent arteriole and the diuretic contracts volume. Incorrect alternatives: This is not an allergy, an embolus, or minimal-change disease, and a doubled creatinine is not a trivial dip.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

scenario: A 59-year-old man with CKD has a potassium of 7.1 mEq/L, peaked T waves, and a widening QRS. Calcium gluconate and insulin-glucose have been given. He is anuric and potassium is still 6.8 mEq/L an hour later. Bicarbonate is 12 mEq/L and he is somnolent.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Another dose of ibuprofen
Urgent dialysis
Oral kayexalate as the only further treatment
Observation overnight
A 2-liter saline bolus
correctAnswer: Urgent dialysis
explanation: Urgent dialysis is correct. Refractory hyperkalemia with QRS widening, anuria, acidosis, and altered mentation is an indication for urgent kidney replacement. Temporizing drugs have already been used. Incorrect alternatives: An NSAID, saline in an anuric patient, overnight observation, and a resin as the only step do not treat membrane toxicity that is not resolving.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

scenario: A 70-year-old man with CKD has a potassium of 6.9 mEq/L. The ECG shows sine-wave QRS widening. He has intravenous access.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate drug?
options: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
Intravenous calcium
Furosemide by mouth
Hemodialysis scheduled for tomorrow morning
A beta blocker
correctAnswer: Intravenous calcium
explanation: Intravenous calcium is correct. Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes when the ECG is already wide. It does not lower the potassium, so shifting and removal follow, but it is the first drug. Incorrect alternatives: A resin, oral furosemide, and next-day dialysis are too slow for a sine wave. A beta blocker does not protect the membrane.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

scenario: A 28-year-old man was found after lying on a floor for 12 hours. The urine is dark and dipstick-positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. Creatine kinase is 48,000 U/L and creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL. Potassium is 5.9 mEq/L.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial fluid plan?
options: Fluid restriction
Vigorous isotonic saline, with monitoring of urine output and potassium
A loop diuretic before any fluid
An NSAID for muscle pain
Immediate renal biopsy
correctAnswer: Vigorous isotonic saline, with monitoring of urine output and potassium
explanation: Vigorous isotonic saline, with monitoring of urine output and potassium is correct. Dipstick blood without red cells plus a very high creatine kinase is rhabdomyolysis. Early volume resuscitation limits pigment injury. Potassium is already high, so fluids are given with a plan for that. Incorrect alternatives: Restriction, a diuretic first, an NSAID, and a biopsy delay or worsen the injury.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 24-year-old man has periorbital and leg edema. Urine protein is 6 g/day, albumin is 2.1 g/dL, and cholesterol is 340 mg/dL. Creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL.
question: Which of the following is the most likely urinary finding that defines this syndrome?
options: Muddy-brown casts
Protein excretion above 3.5 g/day
Red-cell casts as the defining feature
White-cell casts
A post-void residual over 400 mL
correctAnswer: Protein excretion above 3.5 g/day
explanation: Protein excretion above 3.5 g/day is correct. Nephrotic syndrome is heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and often hyperlipidemia. The defining urinary number is protein above about 3.5 g/day. Incorrect alternatives: Muddy-brown casts are tubular injury. Red-cell casts suggest glomerulonephritis. White-cell casts suggest interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis. A residual is obstruction.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 19-year-old man has tea-colored urine 2 weeks after a sore throat. Blood pressure is 162/98 mm Hg. Creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL. Urine shows red-cell casts and protein of 1.2 g/day.
question: Which of the following syndromes best fits?
options: Nephrotic syndrome
Nephritic syndrome
Isolated prerenal azotemia
Chronic urinary retention
Myoglobinuria
correctAnswer: Nephritic syndrome
explanation: Nephritic syndrome is correct. Hypertension, a rising creatinine, cola urine, and red-cell casts with subnephrotic protein are the nephritic pattern, here in the window after pharyngitis. Incorrect alternatives: Nephrotic syndrome is heavier protein and edema without this active sediment. Prerenal labs, retention, and myoglobin do not produce red-cell casts.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 73-year-old man with an eGFR of 32 mL/min/1.73 m2 needs a contrasted CT. He takes lisinopril. He is euvolemic and not in heart failure. A student asks for acetylcysteine because a blog called it protective.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate prevention step?
options: Oral acetylcysteine as the proven preventive drug
Isotonic volume expansion around the contrast exposure, and avoid other nephrotoxins that day
No precautions because contrast never affects the kidney
Start ibuprofen the morning of the scan
Dialysis for every patient with an eGFR under 45 after contrast
correctAnswer: Isotonic volume expansion around the contrast exposure, and avoid other nephrotoxins that day
explanation: Isotonic volume expansion around the contrast exposure, and avoid other nephrotoxins that day is correct. Volume expansion is the prevention step with the best support. Acetylcysteine has not been shown to prevent contrast-associated injury in large trials and is not the plan. Incorrect alternatives: Ignoring risk, adding an NSAID, and dialyzing every stage G3 patient are not appropriate.

references.label: KDIGO CKD Work Group. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD. Kidney Int 2024

scenario: A 30-year-old woman has recurrent pyelonephritis. Ultrasound shows a horseshoe kidney with a stone in the isthmus. She is pregnant and afebrile today, and this visit is for counseling.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate counseling point?
options: A horseshoe kidney has no association with stones or infection
The abnormal drainage raises the risk of stones and infection, so new fever and flank pain need prompt evaluation
The kidney should be removed before any further pregnancy planning
Antibiotics are never used
The finding is a tumor until proved otherwise
correctAnswer: The abnormal drainage raises the risk of stones and infection, so new fever and flank pain need prompt evaluation
explanation: The abnormal drainage raises the risk of stones and infection, so new fever and flank pain need prompt evaluation is correct. Fusion and malrotation impair drainage, so stones and infection are more common. She needs a plan for symptoms, not automatic nephrectomy. Incorrect alternatives: Denying the association, removing the kidney as a first step, forbidding antibiotics, and calling it a tumor are incorrect.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

blueprintTopic: Glyburide is a poor CKD choice
scenario: A 69-year-old man with an eGFR of 24 mL/min/1.73 m2 and type 2 diabetes has hypoglycemia to 48 mg/dL on glyburide. He is not on insulin. Meals are irregular.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate change?
options: Increase glyburide
Stop glyburide; it accumulates in low GFR and causes prolonged hypoglycemia
Add a second sulfonylurea
Start metformin at this eGFR
No change because 48 mg/dL is an acceptable fasting value
correctAnswer: Stop glyburide; it accumulates in low GFR and causes prolonged hypoglycemia
explanation: Stop glyburide; it accumulates in low GFR and causes prolonged hypoglycemia is correct. Glyburide has active metabolites cleared by the kidney and is avoided in advanced CKD. A glucose of 48 is drug toxicity, not a target. Incorrect alternatives: Raising the dose, stacking sulfonylureas, or starting metformin below an eGFR of 30 adds harm.

references.label: American Diabetes Association. 11. Chronic Kidney Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026. Diabetes Care 2026

scenario: A 61-year-old man with newly confirmed heart failure has an ejection fraction of 30%, NYHA class II symptoms, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m2, and potassium 4.3 mEq/L. He is euvolemic. Blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. He takes no heart-failure drugs yet.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying plan?
options: Lisinopril and metoprolol tartrate only, with no mineralocorticoid antagonist or SGLT2 inhibitor
An ARNI or ACE inhibitor, evidence-based beta blocker, mineralocorticoid antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor
Amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide as the four pillars
Diltiazem for rate control of sinus rhythm
Digoxin monotherapy
correctAnswer: An ARNI or ACE inhibitor, evidence-based beta blocker, mineralocorticoid antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor
explanation: An ARNI or ACE inhibitor, evidence-based beta blocker, mineralocorticoid antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor is correct. The 2022 heart-failure guideline uses four drug classes for HFrEF: renin-angiotensin system inhibition (ARNI preferred), an evidence-based beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor. He meets potassium and kidney thresholds and is not volume overloaded. Incorrect alternatives: Two-drug therapy from the older era, dihydropyridine-plus-thiazide as 'pillars,' a non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker, and digoxin alone are not foundational therapy.

references.label: Heidenreich PA et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation 2022

blueprintTopic: Beta blocker in a wet, shocked patient
scenario: A 58-year-old man with known HFrEF arrives in pulmonary edema. Blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg, he is cold and clammy, and lactate is 4.2 mmol/L. He has not been taking his carvedilol for 2 days. A student wants the home dose restarted now.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate beta-blocker decision?
options: Give the full home dose of carvedilol intravenously now
Do not start a beta blocker during cardiogenic shock; stabilize perfusion first
Substitute atenolol
Add diltiazem instead
Start a beta blocker and a calcium blocker together
correctAnswer: Do not start a beta blocker during cardiogenic shock; stabilize perfusion first
explanation: Do not start a beta blocker during cardiogenic shock; stabilize perfusion first is correct. Evidence-based beta blockers save lives in stable HFrEF, but they are not started in a hypotensive, hypoperfused patient. Perfusion is restored first. Incorrect alternatives: An intravenous full dose, atenolol, diltiazem, and a calcium-blocker combination worsen shock or are the wrong drug class.

references.label: Heidenreich PA et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation 2022

scenario: A 66-year-old woman with an ejection fraction of 25% has new atrial fibrillation with a rate of 130/min. Blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and she is warm and mentating. A colleague suggests intravenous diltiazem.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate rate-control choice?
options: Intravenous diltiazem
A beta blocker such as metoprolol, avoiding a non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker
Verapamil
Immediate procainamide because every HFrEF patient has WPW
No rate control is ever used in heart failure
correctAnswer: A beta blocker such as metoprolol, avoiding a non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker
explanation: A beta blocker such as metoprolol, avoiding a non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker is correct. Diltiazem and verapamil are negative inotropes and are avoided in HFrEF. A beta blocker can slow the rate when the patient is perfusing. Incorrect alternatives: Verapamil has the same problem. Procainamide is for pre-excited atrial fibrillation, which is not described. Leaving a rate of 130 untreated is not the alternative.

references.label: Heidenreich PA et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation 2022

scenario: A 70-year-old man with HFrEF has an eGFR of 48 mL/min/1.73 m2 and a potassium of 5.3 mEq/L. He is already on sacubitril-valsartan, carvedilol, and dapagliflozin. Someone orders spironolactone 25 mg.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
options: Start spironolactone and recheck potassium in 6 months
Do not start spironolactone at a potassium of 5.3 mEq/L
Double the dose because the eGFR is under 60
Add ibuprofen to lower potassium
Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor so the spironolactone can be started
correctAnswer: Do not start spironolactone at a potassium of 5.3 mEq/L
explanation: Do not start spironolactone at a potassium of 5.3 mEq/L is correct. Mineralocorticoid antagonists are for HFrEF when potassium is under about 5.0 mEq/L and eGFR is above 30. A potassium of 5.3 is already above that start threshold. Incorrect alternatives: Starting and waiting 6 months, raising the dose, adding an NSAID, or stopping the SGLT2 inhibitor to 'make room' are unsafe.

references.label: Heidenreich PA et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation 2022

scenario: A 54-year-old man was diagnosed with nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy 3 weeks ago. Ejection fraction is 25% on guideline-directed therapy that was just started. He has never had syncope or ventricular tachycardia. He is NYHA class II and euvolemic.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate device plan?
options: Implant a primary-prevention ICD this week
Optimize medical therapy and reassess the ejection fraction after about 3 months before a primary-prevention ICD
Implant a pacemaker for sinus rhythm at 70/min
Start amiodarone indefinitely instead of any reassessment
No medical therapy is needed if a device is planned
correctAnswer: Optimize medical therapy and reassess the ejection fraction after about 3 months before a primary-prevention ICD
explanation: Optimize medical therapy and reassess the ejection fraction after about 3 months before a primary-prevention ICD is correct. Primary-prevention ICD decisions wait until reversible causes are treated and guideline-directed therapy has had time to improve the ejection fraction, generally on the order of 3 months, in a patient with a reasonable survival expectation. Incorrect alternatives: Implanting this week, pacing a normal rhythm, empiric amiodarone, and skipping drugs all skip that reassessment.

references.label: Heidenreich PA et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation 2022

scenario: A 27-year-old man has palpitations. Blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. The ECG shows an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 180/min with beat-to-beat changes in QRS shape. He has a known accessory pathway. He is mentating.
question: Which of the following is the drug to avoid?
options: Procainamide
Ibutilide
AV-nodal blockers such as diltiazem, verapamil, adenosine, or digoxin
Synchronized cardioversion if he becomes unstable
Expert consultation for ablation after the acute episode
correctAnswer: AV-nodal blockers such as diltiazem, verapamil, adenosine, or digoxin
explanation: AV-nodal blockers such as diltiazem, verapamil, adenosine, or digoxin is correct. In pre-excited atrial fibrillation, blocking the AV node can send all conduction down the accessory pathway and accelerate the ventricular rate into fibrillation. Procainamide or ibutilide, or shock if unstable, are the acute options. Incorrect alternatives: Those other choices are appropriate, which is why the node-blocking drugs are the ones that are incorrect here.

references.label: Page RL et al. 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia. Circulation 2016

scenario: An 82-year-old man has exertional syncope. Echo shows a valve area of 0.8 cm2, a mean gradient of 44 mm Hg, and an ejection fraction of 60%. Blood pressure is 138/70 mm Hg. A student wants to 'unload' him with a standing dose of hydralazine.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate direction?
options: Oral hydralazine as definitive therapy
Refer for aortic valve replacement; do not treat severe symptomatic stenosis with vasodilation as the plan
Watch until the ejection fraction falls below 30%
Start a beta blocker to slow the heart to 40/min
Balloon valvuloplasty as a cure
correctAnswer: Refer for aortic valve replacement; do not treat severe symptomatic stenosis with vasodilation as the plan
explanation: Refer for aortic valve replacement; do not treat severe symptomatic stenosis with vasodilation as the plan is correct. Syncope with severe high-gradient aortic stenosis is a replacement indication. Afterload reduction does not fix a fixed obstruction and can drop coronary perfusion. Incorrect alternatives: Waiting for the ejection fraction to collapse, extreme bradycardia, and valvuloplasty as destination therapy are not the guideline plan.

references.label: Otto CM et al. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease. Circulation 2021

scenario: A 44-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve and atrial fibrillation has an INR of 2.2 on warfarin. She asks to switch to apixaban so she can stop checks. She is not pregnant.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
options: Switch to apixaban 5 mg twice daily
Continue warfarin and raise the INR target to 2.5 to 3.5
Aspirin alone
Stop anticoagulation 1 year after valve placement
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily
correctAnswer: Continue warfarin and raise the INR target to 2.5 to 3.5
explanation: Continue warfarin and raise the INR target to 2.5 to 3.5 is correct. A mechanical mitral valve is a warfarin valve. Direct oral anticoagulants are not used. With atrial fibrillation or a mitral prosthesis the INR target is 3, range 2.5 to 3.5, which is higher than her current 2.2. Incorrect alternatives: Apixaban, dabigatran, aspirin alone, and stopping therapy leave the valve unprotected.

scenario: A 33-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation was switched from lisinopril to losartan a week ago at an urgent care visit after a positive pregnancy test. Blood pressure today is 126/76 mm Hg. Potassium and creatinine are normal. She was told an ARB was the safe substitute.

Normal saline from a lab error, so no further thought
Empyema, because glucose is 70
A transudate because glucose is normal

explanation: An exudate, because protein ratio and LDH ratio are both high is correct. explanation: Give alteplase; aspirin use and a remote concussion are not exclusions, and the pressure can be lowered under 185/110 is correct. Single antiplatelet therapy and old minor head trauma are not reasons to withhold. Incorrect alternatives: Heparin is not acute ischemic-stroke treatment. Waiting a day and using NIHSS under 10 as a veto miss the window.

Hemicraniectomy as the first step while she is still following commands
Intravenous heparin

Incorrect alternatives: Warfarin for sinus rhythm, late thrombolysis, no treatment, and lifelong dual therapy are not the plan.

scenario: A 28-year-old man has a painless chancre and a positive treponemal test. He had anaphylaxis to penicillin as a child, confirmed in the record. He has no neurologic symptoms.

No treatment if the chancre is healing
Ceftriaxone ear drops

explanation: Doxycycline for 14 days; reserve penicillin desensitization for pregnancy or neurosyphilis is correct. Azithromycin resistance makes one dose unreliable. A healing chancre and ear drops are not treatment.

Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis
Lactic acidosis from metformin, despite a normal lactate
Starvation with no treatment needed
A lab error because glucose is not 400

explanation: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis is correct. Hold insulin until the potassium is known to be at least 3.3 mEq/L
Give bicarbonate as the only drug

No fluids

scenario: A 32-year-old woman has fatigue, salt craving, and orthostasis. Sodium is 128 mEq/L, potassium is 5.6 mEq/L, and morning cortisol is 2 mcg/dL. ACTH is high. She has hyperpigmented palmar creases.

Levothyroxine before any steroid
Methimazole

explanation: Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone is correct. High ACTH, low cortisol, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia are primary adrenal insufficiency. Liothyronine only

Admit; sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs after dextrose

Insulin infusion

explanation: Admit; sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs after dextrose is correct. Sulfonylureas force insulin release for many hours. Dextrose treats the moment and then glucose falls again. blueprintTopic: Do not use TSH alone early in thyroiditis

A beta blocker and an anti-inflammatory; this is thyroiditis, not Graves
Radioiodine ablation this week
Propylthiouracil
Levothyroxine now while she is thyrotoxic

explanation: A beta blocker and an anti-inflammatory; this is thyroiditis, not Graves is correct. Tender gland, a viral prodrome, and near-zero uptake are subacute thyroiditis. Hormone is leaking, not being made, so antithyroid drugs and ablation do not help. A beta blocker treats symptoms. Isotonic saline
Observation because PTH is suppressed
Lithium
A low-phosphate diet as the only step

explanation: Isotonic saline is correct. Severe hypercalcemia is volume resuscitated first. Suppressed PTH with a lung mass is humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy, not primary hyperparathyroidism, so the cancer pathway is pursued after he is stabilized. scenario: A 66-year-old woman takes metformin. eGFR is 72 mL/min/1.73 m2 and stable. She needs an elective intravenous contrasted CT. She has no acute kidney injury, heart failure, or liver disease.

options: Hold metformin for 48 hours because every contrasted scan requires a hold
Continue metformin; a hold is not required at this eGFR for intravenous contrast
Double the dose the morning of the scan
Switch to glyburide in the scanner
Stop metformin forever because she is over 65
correctAnswer: Continue metformin; a hold is not required at this eGFR for intravenous contrast
explanation: Continue metformin; a hold is not required at this eGFR for intravenous contrast is correct. The FDA hold for iodinated contrast applies when the eGFR is 30 to 60, or when there is liver disease, heart failure, or arterial contrast. The ACR contrast manual does not stop metformin for intravenous contrast when the eGFR is at least 30 and there is no acute kidney injury. At an eGFR of 72 those sources agree she continues it. Incorrect alternatives: Holding every scan, doubling the dose, a sulfonylurea swap, and stopping because of age are incorrect.

Alpha blockade before a beta blocker
A diuretic as the only drug
Immediate biopsy of the mass in the clinic
No blockade is needed
correctAnswer: Alpha blockade before a beta blocker
explanation: Alpha blockade before a beta blocker is correct. Blocking beta receptors first leaves alpha constriction unopposed and can cause a crisis. Alpha blockade, volume restoration, then a beta blocker if the heart rate needs it, is the order before resection. Pressure-lowering drops, acetazolamide, and urgent ophthalmology for laser iridotomy
Topical steroid as the only drug
Oral antibiotic
Patch the eye for 48 hours
correctAnswer: Pressure-lowering drops, acetazolamide, and urgent ophthalmology for laser iridotomy
explanation: Pressure-lowering drops, acetazolamide, and urgent ophthalmology for laser iridotomy is correct. A mid-dilated pupil, a hard globe, and halos are acute angle closure. Pressure is lowered medically and a laser iridotomy is the definitive step. Dilation makes it worse. Incorrect alternatives: A delayed clinic visit, steroid monotherapy, an antibiotic, and a patch do not open the angle.

Emergency stroke-style evaluation; this is a central retinal artery occlusion
Topical antibiotic
Reassurance that a cherry-red spot is viral
A multivitamin
correctAnswer: Emergency stroke-style evaluation; this is a central retinal artery occlusion
explanation: Emergency stroke-style evaluation; this is a central retinal artery occlusion is correct. A pale retina and cherry-red spot are central retinal artery occlusion, an ocular stroke. Same-day ophthalmology for a possible retinal detachment
A 2-week wait
Oral steroid
Antibiotics
correctAnswer: Same-day ophthalmology for a possible retinal detachment
explanation: Same-day ophthalmology for a possible retinal detachment is correct. Flashes, a sudden shower of floaters, and a curtain are retinal detachment until the retina is examined. Central vision can still be saved if the macula is attached. Incorrect alternatives: Tears, a 2-week delay, steroids, and antibiotics do not reattach the retina.

blueprintTopic: Otitis externa and a perforated drum

A fluoroquinolone otic drop; avoid aminoglycoside drops when the drum is open
Oral amoxicillin only, with no drops
Acetic acid and alcohol drops
Steroid drops with neomycin
correctAnswer: A fluoroquinolone otic drop; avoid aminoglycoside drops when the drum is open
explanation: A fluoroquinolone otic drop; avoid aminoglycoside drops when the drum is open is correct. Otitis externa is treated with topical therapy. Aminoglycosides are ototoxic if they reach the middle ear through a perforation, so a fluoroquinolone drop is chosen. Incorrect alternatives: Neomycin combinations, alcohol and acetic acid, and oral therapy alone are the wrong drop or the wrong route.

scenario: A 74-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has severe ear pain, granulation in the canal, and facial-nerve weakness. He is afebrile but looks ill.

Antipseudomonal antibiotics and imaging; this is malignant otitis externa
Antihistamines
Cerumen removal only
Observation
correctAnswer: Antipseudomonal antibiotics and imaging; this is malignant otitis externa
explanation: Antipseudomonal antibiotics and imaging; this is malignant otitis externa is correct. Elderly diabetes, canal granulation, and cranial-nerve involvement are skull-base osteomyelitis, usually Pseudomonas, until proved otherwise. Drops are not enough. Incorrect alternatives: A week of acetic acid, antihistamines, wax removal, and observation miss invasive disease.

scenario: A 19-year-old man has fever, trismus, a muffled voice, and deviation of the uvula away from a swollen tonsil.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Amoxicillin and clinic follow-up next week
Drainage plus antibiotics
Antihistamines
A throat culture only
Steroids as the only drug
correctAnswer: Drainage plus antibiotics
explanation: Drainage plus antibiotics is correct. Uvular deviation, trismus, and a muffled voice are a peritonsillar abscess. It is drained and antibiotics cover group A streptococcus and oral anaerobes. Incorrect alternatives: A delayed oral antibiotic, antihistamines, culture without drainage, and steroids alone do not empty the collection.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 45-year-old man is drooling, sitting forward, and has a fever. He becomes stridorous when examined with a tongue blade. Oxygen saturation is 94%.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Airway specialists in a controlled setting; do not agitate the airway
Oral antibiotics and discharge
A nebulized steroid as definitive care
CT before any airway plan
correctAnswer: Airway specialists in a controlled setting; do not agitate the airway
explanation: Airway specialists in a controlled setting; do not agitate the airway is correct. Drooling and tripoding in an adult are epiglottitis until the airway is secured. Instrumentation in an uncontrolled room can precipitate obstruction. Incorrect alternatives: A forced exam, discharge, a nebulizer as the cure, and a trip to CT before an airway plan are dangerous.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 16-year-old has seasonal sneezing, itchy eyes, and clear rhinorrhea. She has no polyps, asthma, or purulent drainage. She wants something better than as-needed antihistamine tablets.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate controller?

Intranasal corticosteroid
Oral prednisone for the whole season
Pseudoephedrine around the clock in a patient you have not screened for blood pressure
Antifungal tablets
correctAnswer: Intranasal corticosteroid
explanation: Intranasal corticosteroid is correct. Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective single maintenance therapy for allergic rhinitis. Antibiotics and antifungals treat infections she does not have. Incorrect alternatives: A season of prednisone and uncritical decongestant use add harm.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 55-year-old man woke yesterday with hearing loss in the left ear. Weber lateralizes to the right. Rinne shows air greater than bone on the left, and he cannot hear a whispered voice. The canal and drum are normal.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Urgent audiology and prompt corticosteroids for idiopathic sudden sensorineural loss
Antibiotic drops
Cerumen removal
Antihistamines for a month before any test
correctAnswer: Urgent audiology and prompt corticosteroids for idiopathic sudden sensorineural loss
explanation: Urgent audiology and prompt corticosteroids for idiopathic sudden sensorineural loss is correct. Weber to the good ear and a normal exam mean sensorineural loss. Sudden idiopathic loss is treated as an emergency with steroids; delay worsens recovery. Incorrect alternatives: A year of waiting, drops, wax removal, and antihistamines fit conductive problems he does not have.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 7-year-old boy has eyelid swelling, fever, pain with eye movement, and proptosis after a sinus infection. Vision is reduced.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
options: Oral cephalexin for periorbital cellulitis
Intravenous antibiotics and imaging; pain with eye movement and proptosis mean orbital involvement
Antihistamine drops
Warm compresses only
A steroid cream
correctAnswer: Intravenous antibiotics and imaging; pain with eye movement and proptosis mean orbital involvement
explanation: Intravenous antibiotics and imaging; pain with eye movement and proptosis mean orbital involvement is correct. Periorbital cellulitis does not cause proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, or vision loss. Those findings are orbital cellulitis and need intravenous antibiotics, imaging, and often ENT or ophthalmology. Incorrect alternatives: Oral cephalexin, allergy drops, compresses, and a steroid cream under-treat an orbit.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 22-year-old woman has a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL and an MCV of 68 fL. Red-cell count is high for the hemoglobin. Ferritin is 80 ng/mL. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is pending.
question: Which of the following is the more likely pattern?
options: Iron deficiency, because the MCV is low
Thalassemia trait, because the red-cell count is high and ferritin is not low
B12 deficiency
Acute blood loss from yesterday
Sideroblastic anemia from a factory exposure she does not have
correctAnswer: Thalassemia trait, because the red-cell count is high and ferritin is not low
explanation: Thalassemia trait, because the red-cell count is high and ferritin is not low is correct. Iron deficiency has a low ferritin and a low red-cell count. A very low MCV with a high red-cell count and a normal ferritin is thalassemia trait until electrophoresis confirms it. Incorrect alternatives: B12 deficiency is macrocytic. Acute blood loss is normocytic. Sideroblastic anemia is not the default without a toxin.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 66-year-old man on unfractionated heparin for 8 days has a platelet count that fell from 220,000 to 70,000/mm3. He has a new swollen leg. Ultrasound shows a femoral DVT.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next anticoagulant step?
options: Increase the heparin
Stop heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban
Platelet transfusion as the only treatment
Switch to enoxaparin
Warfarin alone tonight with no other anticoagulant
correctAnswer: Stop heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban
explanation: Stop heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban is correct. A platelet fall after day 5 plus a new clot is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia until proved otherwise. All heparin stops, including flushes, and a direct thrombin inhibitor or another non-heparin drug is started. Warfarin is not started alone because of venous limb gangrene. Incorrect alternatives: More heparin, a low-molecular-weight heparin, platelets alone, and warfarin monotherapy propagate the clot.

references.label: NCCPA. Content Blueprint for the PANCE, effective January 2025. NCCPA 2025

scenario: A 35-year-old woman has confusion, a platelet count of 15,000/mm3, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, and hemoglobin 8 g/dL with schistocytes. Coagulation tests are normal. She has no fever.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?

Plasma exchange for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura; do not wait for the full pentad
Heparin
Vitamin K
Observation because she has no fever
correctAnswer: Plasma exchange for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura; do not wait for the full pentad
explanation: Plasma exchange for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura; do not wait for the full pentad is correct. Microangiopathic hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and organ injury with normal coagulation tests are TTP. Fever is often absent. Plasma exchange is started urgently. Platelets are not given unless there is life-threatening bleeding. Incorrect alternatives: Heparin, vitamin K, and observation treat other bleeding disorders.

Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K
Vitamin K by mouth only
Protamine
Idarucizumab
correctAnswer: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K
explanation: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K is correct. Major bleeding on warfarin is reversed with four-factor PCC plus intravenous vitamin K. scenario: Ten minutes into a red-cell transfusion a patient has fever, flank pain, and dark urine. Blood pressure falls.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate first action?

Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with saline
Give another unit faster
Antibiotics and continue the blood
Furosemide and continue
correctAnswer: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with saline
explanation: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with saline is correct. Fever, pain, hypotension, and hemoglobinuria during a transfusion are acute hemolysis until proved otherwise. An inhibitor
Thrombocytopenia
Vitamin K deficiency
A short sample

Dilation and curettage tonight as the only option

Start misoprostol at home with no warning

explanation: Repeat hCG and ultrasound; do not give methotrexate on a single nondiagnostic scan is correct. Azithromycin once

Methotrexate
A blood transfusion

Serotonin syndrome
Malignant hyperthermia from no anesthetic
Sepsis as the only possibility
Catatonia
correctAnswer: Serotonin syndrome
explanation: Serotonin syndrome is correct. Clonus, hyperreflexia, shivering, and a rapid onset after two serotonergic drugs are serotonin syndrome. The combination is required
Lithium toxicity presents only as a rash
No lab is needed

Post it on social media

Trade shifts and say nothing
